title: Waistcoat stitch
subtitle: Inserting between the legs of the V for a knit-fabric look
excerpt: The waistcoat stitch inserts the hook through the centre of the V at the top of each stitch — between the two legs rather than under them — and completes a double crochet. The resulting fabric has visible knit-like columns on both sides and is dense enough to hold its shape without lining.
sourceNotes: Waistcoat stitch technique synthesised from modern crochet teaching. The technique name references its use in structured garments and bags.
heroPrompt: A swatch of waistcoat stitch in cream DK cotton showing the clear knit-like V-columns on both faces of the fabric, natural background.

glossaryTerms.definition: A double crochet worked by inserting the hook through the centre of the V at the top of the stitch (between the two legs) rather than under both loops. Creates a dense, reversible fabric with a knit-like column appearance.

content.text: changes the insertion point of the double crochet from under both top loops to through the centre of the V — between the two legs. That one change makes the fabric look completely different. The stitch draws together tightly, forming a dense, slightly structured fabric with vertical columns that read as knitting.
Work a foundation row of standard double crochet. Turn.

Ch 1. Look at the V at the top of the first stitch. The standard instruction goes under both legs of the V. For waistcoat stitch, aim the hook tip at the centre of the V — through the gap between the two legs.
Push the hook through the centre of the V (through the stitch body, between the two loops).
Complete the double crochet: yarn over, pull through, yarn over, pull through both. The two loops of the V close around the hook shank.
Continue across. The fabric tightens as each row encases the V loops.

attrs.title: Go up one hook size
attrs.body: Waistcoat stitch is tighter than standard double crochet. Work with a hook one size larger than you would normally use for the yarn to compensate for the tighter insertion and keep the fabric supple.

items.symptom: The hook barely fits through the stitch centre
items.cause: The foundation row was too tight, leaving no gap between the V legs.
items.fix: Work the foundation row loose. Use a larger hook for the foundation row and drop to the waistcoat stitch hook on subsequent rows.

items.symptom: The fabric does not show the knit-column effect
items.cause: Inserting under both loops as normal rather than through the V centre.
items.fix: Aim the hook tip directly at the gap between the two legs of the V before pushing through. The hook should exit through the back of the stitch.

content.text: The waistcoat stitch works well in the round for structured bags — worked in continuous spirals with no join, the columns align across every row to create a cohesive fabric. Try a small round base with waistcoat stitches and increase rounds to see how the column pattern holds through shape changes.
